summary: S3 is a low-density nano-bainitic Al–C steel with the highest Al content (8.08 wt.%) of the five-steel series studied in this work. It was austenitized at 1220 °C for 20 min (higher than the 1150 °C used for S1, S2, S4 and S5) and austempered at 270 °C, a temperature just above its measured Ms of 258 °C. The sample represents the extreme high-Al end of the composition window and is used to probe how very high Al and an irremovable residual polygonal-ferrite (αp) fraction govern bainitic transformation kinetics and the strength–ductility trade-off.
composition: Nominal composition (wt.%): C 1.05, Al 8.08, Mn 1.00, Si 0.30, Mo 0.50, B 0.0039; Ni and Ti were not deliberately added. Fe is the balance/base element. S3 carries the highest Al level of the set (3.92–8.08 wt.% range across S1–S5). Al is intended to lower density (≈1.3 % per 1 wt.% Al) and, as a ferrite stabilizer, to accelerate the bainitic transformation, though >9 wt.% Al can cause embrittlement via ordering. The high C (~1.05 wt.%) is required for full austenitization without polygonal ferrite and to keep Ms near ~300 °C. Si (0.30 wt.%) suppresses carbide precipitation and is kept low because Al performs the same role; Mo (0.50 wt.%) and B (0.0039 wt.%) are added to improve hardenability without harming the bainitic transformation. Unlike S4/S5, no Ni (austenite stabilizer) or Ti (microalloying) is present.
processing: Route: vacuum arc furnace casting → homogenization → hot rolling → water-jet cutting → dilatometric heat treatment. Steel blocks were first vacuum arc cast, then homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h under inert argon protection to promote uniform composition and microstructure, then step-by-step hot rolled down to ~11 mm thickness followed by slow cooling in the oven. Samples were precisely fabricated by water jet cutting (OMAX 2626, Kent, Washington, USA) to accurate geometries and minimal thermal distortion; cylindrical specimens (ø5 × 10 mm³) were used in a DIL 805A dilatometer. The heat-treatment cycle followed a common scheme: heating at 10 K s⁻¹ to the austenitizing temperature, an isothermal hold, cooling at 100 K s⁻¹ to the austempering temperature (fast enough to suppress intermediate phase transformations), an isothermal bainitic hold, and a final cooling to room temperature. For S3 specifically, austenitization was at 1220 °C for 20 min; this higher schedule (vs 1150 °C/15 min for S1, S2, S4, S5) was required to minimize αp and approach the simulated ferrite-free field (~1177 °C), although a fully αp-free condition could not be realized within the practical window. S3 was then austempered at TB = 270 °C (just above measured Ms = 258 °C), with an incubation time of 120 s and a slow bainite growth period of nearly 3000 s, the transformation extending to ~43,000 s (Bt). The same alloy was also austempered at 350 °C (Bt ≈ 14,000 s) for comparison.
microstructure: S3 after 1220 °C austenitization and 270 °C austempering develops a multiphase nano-bainitic structure: a bainitic ferrite (αb, bcc) matrix of nanoscale laths forming lenticular sheaves with visible sheaf impingement, plus retained austenite (γr, fcc) at lath boundaries. Quantitative parameters: true lamellar thickness Lt(t) = 40 nm (SD 10 nm); retained austenite Vγ = 29 %; phase-resolved microstrain εγ = 0.54 % vs εα = 0.33 %. Retained austenite includes blocky γr regions between sheaves and partially decomposed, sluggish γr in transformation-free micro-regions. An unavoidable residual polygonal ferrite (αp) fraction of 8.2 % persists (αp was ~14.6 % at the 1050 °C benchmark and could not be removed even at 1220 °C); the ferrite plates are occasionally idiomorphic but predominantly allotriomorphic, and their α versus δ nature remains unclear. Precipitates include (Fe,M)xCy cementite-like carbides (M = Si, Mo; Al essentially absent), located near the γr–bainitic ferrite phase boundaries and only detectable owing to localized SEM brightness; TTP calculation shows a slight increase in (Fe,M)xCy for S3 relative to S1/S2. Nanoscale non-stoichiometric L12-type κ-carbide is presumed embedded in the matrix (not directly observed microscopically, attributed to the limited ~1 wt.% Mn), and AlN particles were also identified by EDX. The enlarged SD of Lt(t) at higher TB (58 nm, SD 23, at 350 °C) reflects coexistence of nB Type 1 and Type 2 alongside blocky γr; at 270 °C the SD narrows (10 nm).
properties: Mechanical/transformation response at TB = 270 °C: UTS ≈1450 MPa with total elongation 2.4 % (PSE ≈3480 MPa·%, i.e. ~3.5 GPa·%) — a severe ductility loss despite the increased strength; Rp0.2 = 945 MPa, the lowest yield strength among all studied steels. Transformation time Bt ≈ 43,000 s at 270 °C versus ≈14,000 s at 350 °C. For reference, at TB 350 °C S3 gave UTS 1360 MPa, El 8.2 % and PSE 11,150 MPa·%. Across the studied alloys overall HV30 hardness ranged 450–500, with higher values at lower TB (except S4). Characterization techniques applied to the steels: dilatometry (DIL 805A), light optical microscopy (LOM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rietveld refinement for Vγ and microstrain following ASTM E975-13), and MatCalc equilibrium/precipitation-kinetics (TTP) simulations; tensile testing on ASTM E8 sub-size round specimens (12.5 mm gauge length, 2.5 mm diameter) with a Zwick/Roell universal machine.
mechanisms: Polygonal ferrite (αp) can act as a nucleation site for bainite, but its low C solubility drives significant C-partitioning into the adjacent austenite; this local C-enrichment stabilizes the austenite and raises the energy barrier around the αp plates, so although initial nucleation is observed at αp–austenite interfaces, bainite growth stalls at many sites, producing transformation-free micro-regions and requiring far longer holds (25,200 s still incomplete; ~43,000 s for near-complete transformation).

Despite Al normally accelerating bainitic transformation and S3 having a short incubation time (~120 s) comparable to S1/S2, the very high Al content (8.08 wt.%) no longer accelerates bainite formation; the marked slowing is attributed to the alloy's dual-phase (αp-containing) microstructure rather than to Al acting as an accelerator.

At the low austempering temperature of 270 °C the phase-resolved microstrain is strongly imbalanced (εγ 0.54 % vs εα 0.33 %), indicating pronounced strain partitioning and dislocation accumulation in the metastable retained austenite; the resulting highly brittle phase boundaries and stress-spiking regions promote early localization and γ→bainitic-ferrite transformation and explain the severe ductility drop to 2.4 %.

Lowering TB from 350 °C to 270 °C refines the true bainitic lamellar thickness from 58 nm to 40 nm and narrows its spread (SD 23 → 10 nm), which raises strength at the cost of ductility — a plate-thickness-mediated strength–ductility trade-off.

S3's Ms of 258 °C is the lowest of the studied steels, consistent with extended κ-carbide dissolution plus ferrite retention that enables local carbon partitioning into austenite, thereby raising the Ms beyond what its very high Al would otherwise dictate; a lower Ms increases the bainitic transformation time.

Rounded, accelerated-nucleation (Fe,M)xCy cementite-like carbides form near γr–bainitic-ferrite boundaries primarily during prior processing/cooling above the austempering temperature (their extremely high nucleation kinetics operate between ~700 and 1150 °C), rather than during the isothermal hold; Si entrapped within the Fe-based carbide lattice and the presence of Mo enhance their stability and inhibit void formation, so they exert negligible influence on tensile properties.

Nanoscale non-stoichiometric L12-type κ-carbide is presumed embedded in the matrix rather than present as detectable plate-like structures, because the limited Mn content (~1 wt.%) is insufficient to stabilize stoichiometric E21-type κ-carbide.
conclusions: S3, with the highest Al content (~8 wt.%) of the series, is the slowest-transforming steel: Bt ranges from 14,000 s (350 °C) to 43,000 s (270 °C), and the delay is attributed to excess stabilization of retained austenite by C-enrichment around polygonal ferrite. Its austenitization demanded the highest schedule (1220 °C, 20 min) and yet could not eliminate αp (8.2 % residual), which is consistent with the ferrite-stabilizing effect of very high Al and the simulated requirement of ~1177 °C to approach a ferrite-free state. At the low austempering temperature of 270 °C, S3 suffers a severe loss of ductility (El ≈ 2.4 %) with only UTS ~1450 MPa, giving the minimum PSE of ~3.5 GPa·% of the study — a strong confirmation of the strength–ductility trade-off driven by pronounced strain partitioning as Ms is approached. Within the tested window the authors conclude that the 8.08 wt.% Al design is detrimental to ductility at lower TB, while C variations near 1 wt.% are secondary to Al level in setting the balance. This makes S3 the benchmark high-Al, slow-kinetics end-member against which the faster Ti-microalloyed S4 and the lower C–Al S5 are compared.
unmapped: S3 was the only steel for which quantitative image analysis of the primary polygonal-ferrite (αp) volume fraction and spatial distribution was performed (ImageJ v1.53, 200× light-optical micrographs from five distinct regions), selected because of its higher αp content.

In S3, carbon quantification in EDX was treated only qualitatively (used to detect (Fe,M)xCy), owing to EDX limitations in carbon measurement; EDX of the S3 particles included Spec.4 (AlN), Spec.5 and Spec.6, with Si and Mo detected in the carbide-like particles.
